chapters.title: Chapter 7: Sector Rotation and Applying Sector Analysis

lessons.title: Sectoral and Thematic Mutual Funds: When They Make Sense and When They Don't

body.text: A sectoral fund asks you to get two decisions right, not one. You must pick the right sector and know when to leave it. A diversified fund manager handles both for you. That is why sectoral and thematic funds belong on the edge of a portfolio, sized deliberately, and almost never as the answer to 'which fund is giving the best returns right now?'

children.text: Most readers of this course invest at least partly through mutual funds, and sectoral and thematic funds are where sector analysis meets real money for you. This lesson covers what these funds actually are under SEBI rules, the specific traps that cost investors money, and the handful of situations where they genuinely earn a place.
What These Funds Are, and What They Are Not

As you saw in Chapter 1, SEBI requires a sectoral or thematic fund to invest at least 80% of its assets in the sector or theme it names. A sectoral fund sticks to one industry, such as banking, pharma, technology, or FMCG. A thematic fund follows an idea that cuts across industries, such as consumption, manufacturing, infrastructure, or public sector companies. A thematic fund is usually a little more diversified than a sectoral one, but it is still a concentrated bet, and it is not a substitute for a diversified equity fund.

body.title: Diversified Fund vs Sectoral or Thematic Fund

columns.label: Diversified equity fund
points: Manager can shift between sectors as the cycle turns
One decision for you: whether to stay invested
Poor performance in one sector is cushioned by others
Suitable as a core, long-term holding

columns.label: Sectoral or thematic fund
points: Manager must stay at least 80% invested in the theme, whatever the cycle is doing
Two decisions for you: when to enter and when to exit
A sector downturn hits the whole fund at once
Suitable only as a small, deliberate satellite position

body.text: Notice the consequence of the 80% rule. Even if the fund manager believes the sector is expensive and heading into a downturn, they cannot move to cash or rotate into a better sector. They can only pick better stocks within the sector. The decision to leave is yours alone, and it is the decision most investors postpone.

children.text: Trap 1: You Usually Hear About Them at the Top

New sectoral and thematic funds are typically launched after a sector has already performed well, because that is when investors are willing to buy them. Fund websites rank categories by past returns, so the best three-year return chart always belongs to whatever has just run up. This means the flow of money into these funds tends to peak close to the point of maximum optimism, which is usually when margins, valuations, and expectations are all elevated, exactly the peak signals you learned to spot in Chapter 2.

body.title: The Arithmetic of a Bad Entry
body.prompt: An investor buys a sectoral fund near a cycle peak. Over the next two years the fund falls 45%. By what percentage must it rise from that level just to get back to the original investment? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: ₹100 falling 45% leaves ₹55. To get back to ₹100, it must rise by 45 ÷ 55 = 81.8%. This asymmetry is why entry price matters so much in concentrated funds. A diversified fund rarely falls this far, but a single sector can, as IT investors found in 2022 and as commodity investors have found in past downturns.

children.text: Trap 2: You May Already Own the Sector

This is the mistake from Chapter 1 that shows up in almost every portfolio review. Your index fund, your large cap fund, and your flexi cap fund all hold the same heavyweight sectors. Adding a sectoral fund on top does not diversify anything; it doubles down. Do the arithmetic before you invest, not after.

body.title: Add Up Your Real Exposure
body.prompt: Ravi has a ₹10,00,000 equity portfolio: ₹6,00,000 in a Nifty 50 index fund with about 37% in financial services, ₹2,00,000 in a banking and financial services fund with 90% in financials, and ₹2,00,000 in a flexi cap fund with 30% in financials. What percentage of his equity portfolio is exposed to financial services? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Index fund: ₹6,00,000 × 37% = ₹2,22,000. Banking fund: ₹2,00,000 × 90% = ₹1,80,000. Flexi cap: ₹2,00,000 × 30% = ₹60,000. Total = ₹4,62,000, which is 46.2% of ₹10,00,000. Nearly half his equity money rides on one sector, and the ₹2,00,000 banking fund is responsible for less than half of that exposure. Most investors in this position believe they are diversified because they hold three different funds.

children.text: When a Sectoral or Thematic Fund Does Make Sense

body.caption: Good Reasons and Bad Reasons to Buy One

cells: The sector is barely represented in your existing funds, such as healthcare or manufacturing
Adds genuinely new exposure rather than concentrating what you already own
You have a specific thesis and the sector trades below its own historical valuation range
You are buying into weak sentiment rather than chasing strength, with a defined reason to hold
You want a small satellite position with pre-set limits and an exit rule
Position sizing controls the damage if you are wrong
It is the top performing category over the last one or three years
Past returns are the most common and most expensive reason investors buy these funds
A new fund offer is being marketed heavily right now
New funds cluster around themes that are already popular and already expensive
You work in the sector and 'understand it well'
Your salary, bonus, and job security already depend on that sector, as you saw in Chapter 1

body.title: Active sectoral fund, index fund, or ETF?

children.text: If you decide you want exposure to a sector, you still have a choice of vehicle. An actively managed sectoral fund lets the manager pick stocks within the sector and usually charges a higher expense ratio. A sector index fund or ETF simply tracks the sector index, such as Nifty Bank or Nifty IT, at a lower cost, but gives you the index's concentration, including its largest constituents in full weight.

Three practical points. First, compare expense ratios, because in a concentrated portfolio, cost differences compound directly against you. Second, check what the fund actually holds; two banking funds can be very different if one leans toward public sector banks and another toward private banks and NBFCs. Third, if you buy an ETF, check trading volumes and how closely its market price tracks its net asset value, since thinly traded ETFs can be expensive to enter and exit.

body.title: The Relationship Manager's Pitch
body.scenario: Your bank's relationship manager calls about a new fund offer: a thematic fund focused on a sector that has been among the market's best performers for three years. The pitch: the theme is backed by a long-term government push, the fund is available at ₹10 per unit so 'the entry price is low', and several colleagues have already invested. You currently hold a Nifty 50 index fund, a flexi cap fund, and a mid cap fund.
body.prompt: How would you evaluate this, and what would you say?
body.modelAnswer: Take the arguments one at a time. A ₹10 net asset value is meaningless: it says nothing about whether the underlying stocks are cheap or expensive, since a new fund always starts at ₹10. Three years of strong performance is a reason for caution, not comfort, because you would be buying after the rerating. A genuine long-term government push may be real, but the question is how much of it is already in the price, so check the theme's current valuation against its own history and whether company earnings have caught up with expectations. Colleagues investing is social proof, not analysis. Then check overlap: add up how much of this theme you already own through your index, flexi cap, and mid cap funds, because the answer is rarely zero. Finally, note that an existing fund with a track record can be assessed on its portfolio and performance, whereas a new fund offer cannot. If after all this you still want exposure, cap it at a small share of your equity portfolio, stagger the investment, and write down in advance what would make you exit.

body.title: Which Investor Is Using These Funds Sensibly?
body.question: Four investors are considering a sectoral or thematic fund. Who is using it most sensibly?
options: Anita puts 40% of her equity money into last year's best performing sectoral fund
Rahul, a software engineer with company stock, adds an IT sectoral fund because he understands the industry
Meera adds a 7% position in a healthcare fund because her index and large cap funds have very little healthcare exposure, and writes down her exit conditions
Suresh invests a lump sum in a new thematic fund offer because the units are priced at ₹10
body.explanation: Meera is adding a sector her portfolio genuinely lacks, sizing it small, and deciding her exit rules before investing. Anita is chasing past returns with a dangerously large position. Rahul is concentrating his portfolio in the same sector that pays his salary and already holds his company stock. Suresh is treating the ₹10 starting price as if it indicated value, which it does not.

body.text: Write your exit conditions down before you invest, in specific terms: a valuation level, a change in the underlying thesis, a time limit, or a target weight you will trim back to. Concentrated positions are easy to enter when everyone is optimistic and very hard to leave when the story is still being repeated on business channels.

body.title: Fill in the Blank
body.textWithBlank: SEBI requires a sectoral or thematic fund to invest at least ___ percent of its assets in its stated sector or theme, which is why the manager cannot rotate away from a weak sector.
body.explanation: The 80% floor is what makes these funds concentrated by design, and it places the timing decision entirely on the investor.

body.title: Before You Invest in Any Sectoral or Thematic Fund
steps: Add up your existing exposure to that sector across all your funds and direct stocks, weighted by the amount you hold in each
Check whether your salary, bonus, or employer stock already ties you to the same sector
Compare the sector's current valuation with its own long-term range, using normalised earnings for cyclicals
Decide the maximum share of your equity portfolio this position may occupy, and stick to it
Choose the vehicle deliberately: active sectoral fund, index fund, or ETF, comparing expense ratios and actual holdings
Stagger your entry over several months instead of investing a lump sum after a strong run
Write down your exit conditions and the tax and exit load consequences of acting on them
Review the position against those written conditions at a fixed interval, not when a headline appears

points: SEBI requires sectoral and thematic funds to keep at least 80% in their stated sector or theme, so the manager cannot rotate away from a downturn
These funds require two correct decisions from you, entry and exit, unlike a diversified fund
New sectoral and thematic funds tend to be launched and bought after a sector has already run, which is the worst time to enter
A 45% fall requires an 81.8% gain to recover, which is why entry valuation matters so much in concentrated funds
Most investors already own their favourite sector through index, large cap, and flexi cap funds; always add up total exposure first
Good reasons to buy: genuinely missing exposure, a valuation-supported thesis, or a small satellite position with rules
Decide position size, vehicle, staggering, and exit conditions before you invest, not afterwards

body.text: This lesson is educational and is not investment advice or a recommendation of any fund or category. Portfolio examples use illustrative figures. Mutual fund investments are subject to market risks; read all scheme related documents carefully. Fund taxation, exit loads, and SEBI categorisation rules can change, so verify current rules before acting.
